> A small electric motor that I design and build from scratch. A 3D-printed rotor carries two neodymium magnets, and a coil of  enamelled copper wire sits next to its path. A Hall sensor detects each magnet as it passes,so the coil pushes the magnet and keeps the rotor spinning. The coil is protected by a flyback diode. I design the schematic in KiCad and the rotor, the coil bobbin and the base in Onshape, and I will build and test it on week 10.

## Design

### 2026-11-07: This week I couldn't think of a cool project, and suddenly it was Wednesday and I still didn't know what to make. Eventually, I decided to build a simple DC motor using some wire, a MOSFET, and a Hall

**2h**

This week I couldn't think of a cool project, and suddenly it was Wednesday and I still didn't know what to make. Eventually, I decided to build a simple DC motor using some wire, a MOSFET, and a Hall sensor. The mechanical parts will be 3D printed, and the motor will be powered by my bench power supply.

I started by drawing the schematic in KiCad. First, I added the power input and a 100 µF capacitor across it. Then I added an IRF9540N MOSFET, an A3144 Hall sensor, a 1N5822 diode, a 10 kΩ resistor, and a coil. I connected everything as shown in the schematic below:

![Zrzut ekranu 2026-11-07 101443](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/f3518f93b43eaa427eb26db3bfe0275e30c47cc91d1afb01b72fb04fbbf3d6a2.png)

The idea is to use the Hall sensor to detect the magnets on the rotor and switch the coil through the MOSFET. I still need to test whether the circuit works as intended.

![obraz_2026-11-07_102253984](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/87ac19934594241438f49f6535127fc2d0feb1734b8796db846fdfe8d0d6d763.png)

Creating the schematic and writing this entry took me about 2 hours. Next, I'll design the rotor, coil holder, and base in Onshape.

### 2026-11-08: ## Week 5, Entry 2: the whole motor in CAD

**4.07h**

## Week 5, Entry 2: the whole motor in CAD

In Entry 1 I chose the idea and drew the schematic. In this session I designed the mechanical part of my motor in Onshape: the rotor, the base, the coil bobbin, the sensor holder and the axis with bearings. Then I put everything together in an assembly and checked how the parts fit. After that I wrote the README and filled in the bill of materials.

### 1. Rotor (time: ~0.4 h)

The rotor is a printed disc, 80 mm in diameter and 8 mm thick, with a hub in the middle. It has:

- a pocket for a 608 bearing on each side (22.1 mm, a little bigger than the bearing, because printed holes come out tight),
- a 16 mm hole through the middle, so that only the outer rings of the bearings touch the rotor,
- two pockets for 10 x 3 mm neodymium magnets on the opposite sides of the axis, 30 mm from the center. Both magnets will have the same pole facing the coil, because  A3144 Hall sensor reacts only to the south pole.

### 2. Base, coil bobbin and sensor holder (time: ~0.6 h)

- **Base:** a 120 x 120 x 8 mm plate with a hole for the axis and four mounting holes.
- **Bobbin:** a printed spool for the coil (about 450 turns of 0.25 mm wire fit between the flanges). Its square peg goes into a square hole in the base, so the bobbin cannot turn.
- **Sensor holder:** a small block with a pocket for the A3144, on the circle of the magnets, 50 degrees before the coil. The sensor must see the magnet before it reaches the coil, so the coil can pull the magnet forward. This position also sets the direction of rotation.

### 3. Axis and bearings (time: ~0,4 h)

The axis is an M8 x 40 bolt with its head sunk into the base. On it there are a 9 mm spacer, the lower bearing, a 2 mm spacer between the bearings, the upper bearing, a washer and a nut. The nut will only be tightened enough to hold the inner rings, so that the rotor spins freely. In Onshape I used a model of the 608 bearing that I found online .

### 4. Mistakes I found and fixed

- The magnet pockets were first 35 mm from the axis, so they were on the very edge of the 80 mm disc. I moved them to 30 mm and moved the bobbin and the sensor to the same distance.
- I first left only a 3 mm gap under the rotor. The coil is about 7 mm high, so the base is now 9 mm below the rotor and a spacer holds the rotor up.
- I first made the hole in the rotor's middle 8.5 mm. The inner ring of the bearing is about 12 mm wide, so it would rub on the spinning rotor. I changed the hole to 16 mm and added a spacer between the inner rings.
- The sensor holder was almost touching the bobbin, so I moved it
- The bolt: I calculated the length from the stack of parts (base, spacer, two bearings, washer, nut) and chose M8 x 40.

### 5. Assembly (time: 0.7h)

![Zrzut ekranu 2026-11-08 124604](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/2c0dd80dc7c3d2648de3459b84337b6b7335506deea365cfd97ffc628713e7a4.png)

I put all parts into an Onshape assembly. The rotor is connected to the base with a revolute mate, so I can turn it around the axis, and the bearings, magnets and rotor move together.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/9ddc8d4093b5ea02c4c757da2beb9ea5ffe4ad71cdf27c58f1d5510e8b29bed3.png)

### 6. README and bill of materials (time: 1h)

I wrote the README in my GitHub repository: how the motor works step by step, the electronics, the mechanical design, safety notes and a progress list. I also added the bill of materials with real prices and vendors. The coil wire, the magnets, the Hall sensors, the MOSFETs, the diodes and the bearings are all inside the $30 budget. (Total: $29.83)
